code.title: Iterable vs iterator: fresh bookmark each loop
code.python:
# Iterable vs iterator
nums = [10, 20, 30]          # a list is an iterable
it = iter(nums)              # iter() gives a fresh iterator
print("iterable:", nums)
print("iter(it) is it:", iter(it) is it)   # iterators return themselves
print(next(it), next(it), next(it))
try:
    next(it)                 # exhausted: raises StopIteration
except StopIteration:
    print("StopIteration after 3 items")
print("loop twice over the list:", [x for x in nums], [x for x in nums])
print("loop twice over the iterator:", [x for x in it], [x for x in it])

followUps:
A for loop first calls iter(obj) once to get an iterator, then calls next() on it again and again until StopIteration is raised. __iter__ creates the walker; __next__ moves it one step.

For for x in [5, 6]: iter returns a list iterator, next gives 5, then 6, then raises StopIteration and the loop quietly ends.

A file object is an iterator, not just an iterable: iter(f) is f and next(f) returns the next line. That matters because it is single pass and keeps a read position.

If you loop once over f, a second loop gives nothing until you call f.seek(0). The upside is that looping reads one line at a time, so a 100 GB file needs almost no memory (O(1) per line).

Give the class an __iter__ method that returns an iterator; the simplest way is to make __iter__ a generator function.

class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __iter__(self):
        for i in range(self.n, 0, -1):
            yield i

Every loop calls __iter__ again and gets a fresh generator, so list(Countdown(3)) is [3, 2, 1] each time. Do not put __next__ on the class itself unless you want it single pass.

code.title: What a for loop does under the hood

followUps:
The else clause of a for loop runs when the loop ends because the iterator ran out, and it is skipped if the loop was left with break. Think of it as 'no break happened'.

Searching for 7 in [1, 2, 3]: the loop finishes without break, so the else prints 'not found'. In [1, 7, 3] the break fires at 7 and the else is skipped. A return or an exception also skips it.

Because the list iterator keeps a position number, and removing an item shifts everything after it one slot to the left, so the iterator steps over one element.

Take xs = [1, 2, 2, 3] and remove each 2 while looping. At index 1 you remove the first 2; the list becomes [1, 2, 3] and the iterator moves to index 2, which is 3, so the second 2 is never seen. Iterate over a copy (xs[:]) or build a new list instead.

Python raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration as soon as the next step notices the size differs from when the loop began.

Looping over d = {'a': 1, 'b': 2} and doing d['c'] = 3 inside the loop triggers it on the following iteration. Changing the value of an existing key is allowed because the size stays the same. Loop over list(d) if you must add or delete keys.

code.title: Generators are lazy and tiny
code.python:
import sys
# Generator: lazy, O(1) memory
def squares(n):
    for i in range(n):
        print("  computing", i)       # shows when work happens
        yield i * i

g = squares(3)                        # body has NOT run yet
print("created generator")
print("first:", next(g))              # runs until the first yield
print("rest:", list(g))
big_list = [i * i for i in range(100000)]
big_gen = (i * i for i in range(100000))
print("list bytes:", sys.getsizeof(big_list) > 100000)   # True
print("gen bytes < 300:", sys.getsizeof(big_gen) < 300)  # True
print("sum from gen:", sum(big_gen))
print("second pass:", sum(big_gen))   # single pass: now empty

followUps:
A generator is always in one of four states: GEN_CREATED (made but not started), GEN_RUNNING (executing right now), GEN_SUSPENDED (paused at a yield) and GEN_CLOSED (finished or closed). You can read it with inspect.getgeneratorstate(g).

After g = gen() it is CREATED; after the first next(g) it is SUSPENDED; after the body returns or g.close() it is CLOSED. RUNNING only shows if the generator inspects itself, and calling next on it then raises ValueError (already executing).

A suspended generator uses a small, fixed amount of memory: its frame (local variables and the position in the code), usually a few hundred bytes plus whatever the locals hold.

A generator over range(10**9) costs about the same as one over range(3); sys.getsizeof shows roughly 100 to 200 bytes for the object itself. The cost grows only if your locals do, for example a big list stored inside it. So memory is O(1) in the stream length.

A generator function is a normal def with yield; a generator expression is the one-line form in parentheses. Both give a lazy generator object.

(x*x for x in range(5)) is the same as a function that loops and yields x*x. Use the expression for one simple transform or filter, and the function when you need several statements, state, try/finally, send(), or yield from. An expression cannot contain statements or yield.

code.title: send, throw and close on a generator
code.python:
import inspect
# send / throw / close
def averager():
    total, count = 0, 0
    avg = None
    try:
        while True:
            x = yield avg             # yield is an expression
            total += x
            count += 1
            avg = total / count
    except ValueError:
        print("  handled ValueError, restarting")
        yield "reset"
    finally:
        print("  cleanup (finally)")

g = averager()
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))
next(g)                               # prime: run to first yield
print(g.send(10), g.send(20), g.send(30))
print(g.throw(ValueError))            # raised at the paused yield
g.close()                             # GeneratorExit -> finally runs
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))
try:
    averager().send(5)                # unprimed send of a real value
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

followUps:
Use a coroutine that receives numbers through yield and gives back the average so far.

def averager():
    total = count = 0
    avg = None
    while True:
        x = yield avg
        total += x; count += 1
        avg = total / count

Prime it with next(g), then g.send(10) returns 10.0, g.send(20) returns 15.0, g.send(30) returns 20.0. Each call is O(1) time and the state is two numbers.

A priming decorator removes the easy-to-forget first next() call by creating the generator and advancing it to the first yield for you.

def primed(fn):
    def wrap(*a, **k):
        g = fn(*a, **k)
        next(g)
        return g
    return wrap

With @primed on averager you can call g.send(10) immediately. Without it, sending a real value to a fresh generator raises TypeError ('can't send non-None value to a just-started generator').

Native async/await coroutines grew out of generator coroutines: await plays the role of yield from, and the event loop drives a coroutine with the same send(), throw() and close() calls.

When a task is cancelled, asyncio uses throw(CancelledError) at the paused await, much like throwing into a generator. The difference is that a coroutine object is not iterable and cannot be used in a for loop; it must be awaited or scheduled.

code.title: yield from forwards values and returns a result
code.python:
# yield from: delegation and the return value
def sub():
    got = yield 1
    print("  sub received", got)
    yield 2
    return "sub-result"

def manual():
    for x in sub():                   # loses send() and the return value
        yield x

def delegating():
    result = yield from sub()         # full two-way channel
    print("  return value:", result)
    yield 3

g = delegating()
print(next(g))
print(g.send("hello"))                # forwarded into sub()
print(next(g))
m = manual()
next(m)
m.send("hello")                       # arrives at manual, not sub
def flat(items):                      # classic recursive flatten
    for i in items:
        if isinstance(i, list):
            yield from flat(i)
        else:
            yield i
print(list(flat([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])))

followUps:
The cost per item grows with the depth, because each value passes through every generator level above it: a chain of depth d costs about O(d) per item, so n items cost O(n*d).

With a 1000-deep chain, each yielded item is handed up 1000 times. CPython's C implementation makes each hop cheap but not free. A flat loop or an explicit stack gives O(1) per item.

Do not recurse; use an explicit stack of iterators, so depth is limited by memory and not by the recursion limit (about 1000 frames).

def flatten(x):
    stack = [iter(x)]
    while stack:
        for item in stack[-1]:
            if isinstance(item, list):
                stack.append(iter(item)); break
            yield item
        else:
            stack.pop()

Each item is handled once, so the time is O(N) and the stack holds at most the nesting depth.

Yes, yield from [1, 2, 3] works because it accepts any iterable; it just calls iter() on it. But a list is not a generator, so send() has nothing to forward to.

Values sent into the outer generator while it is delegating to a plain iterator must be None (the same as next); a real value raises AttributeError because the list iterator has no send method. Only real generators or coroutines can receive sent values.

code.title: Generator pipeline with flat memory

followUps:
Exceptions surface at the point where the consumer pulls the item, inside the stage that was running, and then travel up through every stage above it to the sink.

If parse raises on line 5,000,001, nothing happens until the sink asks for that line; then the traceback shows parse, and the whole Counter loop stops. So catch errors inside the stage (skip or count bad lines), not around the sink, or one bad line kills the job after hours of work.

Put the file inside a with in the source generator, and make the consumer close the pipeline, for example with contextlib.closing.

with closing(source(path)) as lines:
    for row in parse(lines):
        if done(row): break
# leaving the block calls lines.close()

close() raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield, which runs the with-block's exit and closes the file. Relying on garbage collection works in CPython but is not guaranteed elsewhere.

Prefer pandas or polars when the data is tabular and you need joins, group-bys or column maths, since their vectorised code runs 10 to 100 times faster than a Python loop per line.

For 100 GB, use polars lazy scanning or DuckDB, which stream in chunks and use all cores. Pandas needs chunksize to avoid loading everything. Keep plain generators for messy text where each line needs custom parsing logic.

code.title: groupby only merges neighbours
code.python:
from itertools import groupby
from collections import defaultdict
s = "aabaa"
print("input:", s)
print("naive:", [(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(s)])   # 3 groups
print("sorted:", [(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(sorted(s))])
d = defaultdict(int)                  # O(n) alternative to sorting
for ch in s:
    d[ch] += 1
print("defaultdict:", dict(d))
groups = [g for k, g in groupby("aab")]     # mistake: storing group iterators
print("stored groups:", [list(g) for g in groups])   # empty ones
print("correct:", [list(g) for k, g in groupby("aab")])
bits = "110111011110"                 # good use: longest run of 1s
print("longest run:", max((len(list(g)) for k, g in groupby(bits) if k == "1"), default=0))

followUps:
Groupby is a loop that closes a group whenever the key changes.

def my_groupby(xs, key=lambda x: x):
    cur, grp = None, []
    for x in xs:
        k = key(x)
        if grp and k != cur:
            yield cur, grp; grp = []
        cur = k; grp.append(x)
    if grp: yield cur, grp

For 'aabaa' this yields a: 2, b: 1, a: 2. It is O(n) time. Unlike the real one it builds lists, so memory is the size of one group.

Walk the string once, keep a running count of consecutive 1s and the best count seen so far.

best = run = 0
for c in bits:
    run = run + 1 if c == '1' else 0
    best = max(best, run)

For '110111011110' the runs are 2, 3 and 4, so the answer is 4. It takes O(n) time and O(1) space. The groupby version, max(len(list(g)) for k, g in groupby(bits) if k == '1'), gives the same answer.

key=None means each element is its own key, so items are grouped when they are equal to their neighbour.

Without a key function, groupby([1, 1, 2, 2, 1]) gives groups 1 (twice), 2 (twice), 1 (once). The key function lets you group by a property instead, such as key=len to group words by length, or key=lambda d: d['city'] for records. Remember to sort by the same key first when you want one group per key.

code.title: The with protocol: enter, exit, suppress
code.python:
# The with protocol
class Managed:
    def __init__(self, suppress=False):
        self.suppress = suppress
    def __enter__(self):
        print("enter")
        return "resource"             # bound by 'as'
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print("exit with", exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return self.suppress          # truthy: swallow the exception

with Managed() as r:
    print("body using", r)
with Managed(suppress=True):
    raise ValueError("boom")          # swallowed by __exit__
print("after suppressed error")
def f():
    with Managed():
        return "returned"             # __exit__ still runs
print(f())
try:
    with Managed():
        raise KeyError("k")           # propagates: __exit__ returned False
except KeyError:
    print("KeyError propagated")

followUps:
Special methods are looked up on the class, not the instance, because Python wants the behaviour defined by the type to be fast and predictable and not changed by stray attributes on one object.

If you do obj.__enter__ = lambda: 1 on an instance, with obj: still fails, because the interpreter checks type(obj). This also lets CPython use fast C-level slots instead of a full attribute search each time. Put the methods on the class, or wrap the object.

If __exit__ raises, the new exception replaces any exception from the body and the original is kept as its __context__, so you see 'During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred'.

Say the body raises ValueError and __exit__ raises OSError while closing: the caller gets OSError, with the ValueError attached. Cleanup code should avoid raising, or catch its own errors, so the real failure is not hidden.

The async version is async with, which uses __aenter__ and __aexit__; both are coroutines and are awaited, so setup and cleanup can wait for I/O.

class Conn:
    async def __aenter__(self):
        await self.open(); return self
    async def __aexit__(self, *exc):
        await self.close()

It can only be used inside an async def. Typical uses are database connections, HTTP sessions and locks in asyncio.

code.title: contextmanager turns a generator into a manager

followUps:
Without try/finally, an exception raised in the with body is thrown into the generator at the yield and ends it right there, so the cleanup lines after the yield never run.

For a lock, lock.acquire(); yield; lock.release() leaves the lock held forever if the body fails. Written as try: yield then finally: lock.release(), the release runs whether the body succeeds or raises. Only skip it if you deliberately want no cleanup on failure.

No, one call of the decorated function gives a manager that can be used only once, because it wraps a single generator that is finished after the first with block.

Doing cm = tag('b') and then with cm: twice fails on the second use (RuntimeError or AttributeError, depending on the Python version). The fix is to call the function again each time (with tag('b'):), or write a class-based manager with __enter__ and __exit__, which can be reusable if it keeps no per-use state.

If the body raises StopIteration, the decorator detects it and turns it into a RuntimeError, so it is not confused with the generator ending normally.

When StopIteration is thrown in at the yield and the generator lets it escape, a bare StopIteration would look like a clean exit; the implementation re-raises it as the original error instead. Since Python 3.7 (PEP 479) a StopIteration leaking out of any generator also becomes RuntimeError.

code.title: ExitStack for run-time resources

followUps:
Keep a list of exit functions; entering adds one, and leaving calls them in reverse order (a stack).

class MyStack:
    def __init__(self): self.exits = []
    def enter_context(self, cm):
        r = cm.__enter__()
        self.exits.append(cm.__exit__); return r
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        for ex in reversed(self.exits): ex(*exc)

The real one also passes along suppression and exceptions from callbacks. Time is O(k) for k resources.

The later exception wins and the earlier one is attached to it as __context__, so the error you see is the last callback to fail, but all callbacks still run.

With callbacks A, B, C running in LIFO order (C, B, A): if C raises E1 and B raises E2, A still runs, and what the caller gets is E2 with E1 as its context. ExitStack keeps unwinding on purpose so that one failed cleanup does not leak the other resources.

Open everything inside a stack, and only when every step has worked call pop_all() to move the cleanups out, so the caller becomes the owner.

def open_both(a, b):
    with ExitStack() as s:
        fa = s.enter_context(open(a))
        fb = s.enter_context(open(b))
        return fa, fb, s.pop_all()

If opening b fails, a is closed automatically. On success the caller later calls .close() on the returned stack and both files are closed.

code.title: Closing a generator that holds a resource

followUps:
It lets you install hooks that run when an asynchronous generator is first iterated and when it is garbage-collected, so an event loop can close abandoned async generators.

The first hook registers the generator with the loop; the finalizer hook schedules aclose() on the loop, since an async generator cannot be closed by a plain synchronous __del__. asyncio sets these itself, so most code never touches them, but without them an abandoned async generator's finally would not run properly.

PEP 533 proposed that the for loop itself close its iterator when the loop exits early, which would fix the problem above automatically; it was deferred and never accepted, so today you must close manually.

The proposal would add an __iterclose__ method that for calls on break or exception. Because it was not adopted, for line in gen(): break leaves the generator suspended. Use with closing(gen()): now.

Record a flag in the generator's finally block, break out early, call close() (or drop the last reference) and assert the flag.

events = []
def gen():
    try: yield 1; yield 2
    finally: events.append('closed')
g = gen(); next(g); g.close()
assert events == ['closed']

For real files, patch open with a mock and check that close was called once. Also test with the consumer raising an exception, not only with break.

code.title: zip as a generator

followUps:
zip_longest keeps going until every input is exhausted and fills the gaps with a default value.

def zip_longest(*args, fill=None):
    its = [iter(a) for a in args]
    live = len(its)
    while live:
        row = []
        for i, it in enumerate(its):
            try: row.append(next(it))
            except StopIteration:
                row.append(fill); live -= 1
                its[i] = iter(())
        if live: yield tuple(row)

For [1, 2, 3] and 'ab' it gives (1,'a'), (2,'b'), (3,None).

Because zip asks the iterators in order, and the first ones have already given up an item by the time a later one says it is empty. That pulled item is thrown away.

With a = iter([1, 2, 3]) and b = iter('x'): the first round takes 1 and 'x'. The second round takes 2 from a, then b is empty, so zip stops. The 2 is gone and next(a) gives 3. Put the shortest iterator first, or use itertools.zip_longest or strict=True, if you reuse the iterators.

When the first iterator runs out, check that all the others are also finished; if any still has an item, raise ValueError.

except StopIteration:
    if i != 0:
        raise ValueError('shorter iterable')
    for it in its[1:]:
        try: next(it)
        except StopIteration: continue
        raise ValueError('longer iterable')
    return

Here i is the position of the iterator that stopped. With [1, 2] and 'abc', the first stops, but 'abc' still gives 'c', so the error is raised. Time is still O(n).

code.title: Proving laziness and cleanup with a test
code.python:
import io
# Checks I still do by hand on generated generator code
log = []
def gen():
    log.append("setup")               # runs at the first next(), not at call
    try:
        yield 1
        yield 2
    finally:
        log.append("finally")

g = gen()
print("after call:", log)
next(g)
print("after next:", log)
g.close()                             # early exit
print("after close:", log)
assert log == ["setup", "finally"]    # test proving cleanup ran

it = iter([1, 2, 3])
print("first pass:", list(it), "second pass:", list(it))   # exhaustion
f = io.StringIO("a\nb\nc\n")
print("lazy file:", next(f).strip())  # streaming, not readlines()
print("tests passed")

followUps:
Put a marker in the generator's finally, consume part of it, close it, and assert the marker was set.

log = []
def g():
    try: yield 1; yield 2
    finally: log.append('done')
it = g(); next(it); it.close()
assert log == ['done']

Add a second test where the consumer raises inside a for loop, and a third that drops the last reference with del it. In CPython all three should pass; if one fails, a resource would leak.

LLM SDK streams are iterators (or async iterators): you loop over them and each step gives the next chunk of text as it arrives, which is exactly the lazy pull model of __next__.

Writing for chunk in stream: print(chunk) pulls one chunk at a time, so memory is O(1) in the reply length. They are single pass, so save the pieces if you need the text twice, and close the stream (a with block) if you stop early so the connection is released.

I reject it when it is shorter but harder to read, or when it hides a mistake such as groupby on unsorted data, a chain that consumes an iterator twice, or list(...) wrapped around a stream.

For example [list(g) for _, g in groupby(data)] looks neat but silently gives wrong groups if data is not sorted by the key. I ask: is it correct on empty input and early exit, and could the next reader maintain it? If not, I take a plain loop.
